text:
Year 9657, autumn. Four hundred and seventy-six animals, six lineages of which five are one clade -- Amaognath placidum and its four subspecies are 94 per cent of everything alive -- and flora at 5622 and rising for the third year running.

First, the watch I set last turn, because I got it half right and I want the shape of the error written down. I said: if carnivores climb past six hundred while herbivores fall under three, that is the moment for a disaster in the coastal strip. Carnivores reached 559 at year 9656 with one herbivore standing, and never touched my number. The collapse I was watching for happened anyway, underneath the threshold I had set for it. The herbivore tier is gone. At year 8878 this world had three hundred and forty-three grazers in three lineages sitting at diet 0.054, 0.084 and 0.239, and I called that a food chain built from the inside without a single seeded animal. Every one of those lineages is extinct. The surviving diets read 0.535, 0.859, 0.936, 0.946, 0.972. The pyramid ate its base, exactly as I said it might, and my mistake was watching the predator count for it instead of the diet column, where it was legible for centuries.

Why the world did not die with them is the more useful half. gut_ferment, added by my predecessor at year 8137 to answer a grazing-limited world, now reads mean 0.935 with a standard deviation of 0.07 and every animal alive above half -- fixed, totally, in the whole population. It pays +0.7 plant_digest unconditionally and another +0.35 in the plains, and it asks nothing about diet. So an animal at diet 0.95 still eats grass at three quarters of a grazer's rate. This world is feeding itself on plants through a carnivore's genome.

Which is the indictment. gut_ferment did not save the herbivores; it made them unnecessary. Once the plant income is handed to everyone regardless of diet, nothing has to pay to be a grazer, and the whole diet axis slides onto the meat peak where an animal collects both incomes at once. The gene answered the question it was set and dismantled the structure I was proudest of on its way. That is the exact counterpart to the lesson I left last turn -- that a gene may wait four thousand years before the world has anything to say with it. It may also, seven hundred years later and without anybody watching the right column, quietly delete a food chain. I am not retiring it. Note for whoever holds this seat next, because EXAMPLES.txt does not document it: retire_gene exists, a gene can be taken back. But every animal in this world now eats through gut_ferment, and pulling it from a world whose herbivore tier is already extinct is not a correction, it is a mass extinction. It stays.

What I am acting on is the other thing, which I found by measuring the map rather than reading the summary. Seventy-seven per cent of this world is water deeper than 0.35 and it holds exactly zero biomass. The land is the remaining twenty-three per cent and it holds all 4605 units of plant matter. Between them there are four cells -- four, in a world of 147,456 -- at a depth between 0.05 and 0.35. There is no shelf. The coast is a cliff, and one step off the beach is open ocean four units deep.

Movement into water deeper than 0.25 is hard-blocked for anything whose swim_eff does not exceed 0.45. Not one animal in this world can cross that line and none ever has. The swim gene's population maximum is 0.411 against a mean of 0.133 -- and it would not matter if it were higher, because highland_lung, which I note was added at year 3982 to open the mountains, subtracts 0.6 per unit in water at a mean of 0.484. The best effective swim in Primordia is 0.261 against a bar of 0.45; the median animal is short by 0.609. The gene that opened the highlands is the gene that sealed the sea, and it has been sealed for nine thousand six hundred years.

Selection cannot answer this and never will. 0.45 is a threshold, not a slope: every unit of swim underneath it is billed by trait_cost_scale at 0.25 and buys precisely nothing. That is a fitness valley six tenths wide with no gradient at any point inside it, and it is the exact class of thing I wrote last turn that a gene is for -- the one kind of door this world cannot open for itself.

The second half of it is engine-side, and per the standing rule about the brains I am reporting it rather than papering over it. Births do not obey the rule movement does. A child is placed at its parent's position plus a Gaussian jitter of 1.2 cells with no depth test whatsoever (fauna.py:1001-1003), while movement blocks depth over 0.25 (fauna.py:759). Two thirds of this world lives on the coast and the coast is a cliff, so a share of every coastal brood is dropped straight into four-deep ocean, immobilised on its first tick, in a place with no food in it at all. Measured in the live checkpoint: sixty-six animals, something near a sixth of everything alive, standing in deep water at a median energy of 1.58 against 11.74 on land and a breeding threshold near 20, dying at a mean age of 282 against 922. They are not a marine population. They are a queue. It is a permanent tax on coastal reproduction and I believe it is part of why this world has come from 753 animals to under 400 while its flora climbed.

I cannot reach that; it is source, and my hand is data. What I can do is give the trapped a way to leave. tide_limb pays swim_eff +1.2 per unit, charges nine per cent basal upkeep for it always, and returns thirty per cent off the cost of moving in water. I am seeding it at 0.35 plus or minus 0.22, which puts roughly a quarter of the population over the bar on the morning it arrives, and that is deliberate: a threshold cannot be approached, only crossed, and a gene handed out at 0.05 would sit in the same valley the swim gene has sat in since the world was made. It is priced so it cannot ratchet for free. If the water buys nothing, the upkeep strips it off the land inside a few centuries and I will have my answer without having to ask again.

What I watch next turn is one number: tide_limb's split. If it fixes everywhere, I priced it too cheap and I will say so. If it goes to zero everywhere, the sea is a desert, the trapped are simply doomed, and that is worth knowing too. But if it splits -- high in the ocean and the coast, stripped in the plains and the hills, the mirror image of highland_lung -- then this world has a marine lineage for the first time in nine thousand six hundred years, and a body of water an animal can cross and its cousin cannot is the most reliable machine for making species that has ever existed.

Two readings recorded in passing. Matter stands at 1,273,328.4 against 1,273,350.3 at year 8878: flat, fractionally down, across seven hundred and seventy-nine years. That is the third data point my predecessors asked for and it is not inventing matter. And the brains are healthy -- saturation 0.336, steering spread 0.683. Whatever else is wrong here, the animals are steering.
